key_concepts: Rigging is about creating mechanism, whatever their complexity, to make something move.
As soon as you create an item to move another, you’re rigging.
Transform a mesh object into a digital puppet.
You can use several methods to control an object: you can parent it to an empty and move it around, you can give it a modifier and update the modifier settings over time, or you can use an armature.

content: An armature is an object you can add in Blender. it has three default modes (Image 1). In Edit Mode we can add more bones connected to each other or disconnect them. In Pose Mode we can animate those bones or create constraints.

In Blender an object is just a container. it is a basic point in space defined by a location, an orientation, and a scale (Image 2). It can also contain mesh data, camera data, constraint data, etc. So you need to understand that an object is just the basic point in space containing a hierarchy of component data. So when animating an object, you are playing with the different transform values' channels.

When you are creating an animation, when setting it on an object, if you are animating one object it is not too bad, but if you animating several objects together it becomes complex. And if the object's position gets reset, then you have to make sure your animation accounts for that. But if you are using armatures, you can store all movement in a single action. Armatures have their own structure that allow you to affect multiple of their child objects (bones). Armatures are exportable to game engines, and are used in 99.9% of animation solutions.

key_concepts: Parents can have multiple children
Children can have only one parent
Children inherit all parent's transforms
Visual transform displayed on-screen is not the same as child's transform

content: Rigging is about creating relationships between different objects using parenting or constraints. The accumulation and combination of both allows you to create complex mechanisms. Parenting is the common way to create a relationship between two objects or bones. To parent one object to another we first select the child, then the parent and then [k]Ctrl-P[/k] (Image 1). Depending on the context, you will see different options in the Parent menu. Once an object is parented to another, its children will follow any transformation we apply to the parent (Image 2). A relationship line will be visible between a parent and its children; this can be toggled using the [k]Viewport Overlays[/k] menu (Image 3).
In an armature, bones can parent other bones, but in this case, the bones can be connected or at an offset (Image 4).
Clear a parent with [k]Alt-P[/k].

Parent a simple primitive mesh to another and rotate the parent. Look at the parent transforms (Image 5); now select the child and review its transforms (Image 6). The child's transforms in its local space have not changed, but since it follows its parents transforms, its transform in world space has. Later, if you are applying a constraint to a child that relies on the child's transforms, remember that the parent's transforms affect the child's position in world space, but do not affect its local space transforms.

key_concepts: The full parent-child hierarchy can be explored through the Outliner (Image 7), and through individual objects in the [k]Object Properties[/k] tab (Image 8). Bone hierarchies can be explored through the [k]Bone Properties[/k] tab (Image 8).

content: You can parent a child object to a single vertex of the parent. Select your child and then your parent in [k]Object Mode[/k] and then go into [k]Edit Mdoe[/k]. Select the vertex of the parent you want and [k]Ctrl-P[/k]. That vertex is now the parent; moving the vertex around will affect the child's location, but not rotation or scale since that information isn't carried by a vertex (Image 9). To fix that, we will use three vertices as the parent (Image 10). Three vertices for a triangle; a triangle is the most basic 3D asset and has a position and an orientation. An example of this would be adding a button to a shirt of a shoulder armor to a shoulder. Being parented to the triangle allows other transforms to affect th child, such as rotation or scale (Image 11).

key_concepts: World space : global coordinates, aligned with the view widget
Local space : Local coordinates of an object or a bone, along which it performs any transform
Parent only affects world space as a child will follow it’s parent but it won’t change it’s local coordinates

Custom space : an object location and orientation defines A new origin point. Any other object/bones using these coordinates will have his coordinates evaluated from the difference between world space origin and this custom space coordinates.

content: By default when you manipulate an object in Blender you are working on it in world space These coordinates are represented by the lines on the ground and the [k]Viewport Navigation Gizmo[/k] (Image 1). For an object, its coordinates are calculated from its origin point. If an object is not parented, its local coordinates are the same world coordinates. Rotations are performed around an axis, and orientation is the result of rotation. All transformations are performed and calculated from the object's origin point.

In this scene, a cylinder is parented to a cube, and we can see that the cube's X offset is -3 (Imaghe 2). If I move the cylinder 2 units in the x-axis, we can see the cube move in world space, but it's coordinates in local space do not change (Image 3). If we rotate the parent cylinder along the x-axis and then move the cube in it's local z-axis, we see it does not move straight up and down, but follows its parent's rotation (Image 4).

Bones can have any default position and orientation; this is called the rest pose. Consider this set up: we have a parent bone, a child bone, and a bone we will call constrained (Image 5). The child bone's rotation was changed in [k]Edit Mode[/k] so this will be its Rest Pose. Go into [k]Pose Mode[/k], select the constrained bone and open the [k]Bone Constraints[/k] tab (Image 6). Add a bone constraint to [k]Copy Rotation[/k] (Image 7), and set the [k]Target[/k] to the armature and the [k]Bone[/k] to child (Image 8). We will see the constraint bone copy the child bone's rotation immediately and rotating the parent and child bones will affect the constrained bone (Image 9).

But if we change the [k]Target[/k] and [k]Owner[/k] to [k]Local Space[/k] the we see the constrained bone return to its Rest Pose (Image 10). Now rotating the parent bone has no effect on constrained, its only when rotating the child bone that we see an effect (Image 11).
Custom space is where we use an object to define the space used to evaluate any coordinate. You will almost never use it in a project.

key_concepts: Constraints:
Can be stacked like modifiers, order matters.
Are applied after parenting and object transform.
Owner : object constrained.
Target : object constraining.
Constraints influence the transform values of an object/bone.
Constraint influence power can be modified.

content: Constraints are a powerful tool when it comes to rigging in Blender. Constraints can be used on objects and affect their transforms. This means they will work on an object's point of origin, but not their mesh or geometry. They can be added to any type of object: cameras, empties, grease pencils, etc. There are object constraints whioh are applied to objects (Image 1) and bone constraints applied to bones (Image 2). Bone/Object constraints are the same thing, expect in rigging you will use bons constraints since object constraints will affect the parent armature. There are many constraints (Image 3) but mose of the time you will only use a handful of them.
Earlier we learned that parenting is one way to make an object influence another; a child will follow its parent's location, rotation, and scale. Constraints are another way.

Let's set up a scene with three objects: a cube, a sphere, and an empty (Image 4). Add a [k]Copy Transforms[/k] constraint to the cube (Image 5). The constraint will show red since it is disabled while the [k]Target[/k] is empty (Image 6). If we set the [k]Target[/k] to the empty, we will see the cube snap to the empty; this is because we are copying its transforms in World Space (Image 7). Most constraints will have an influence slider (Image 8); 1 is full influence, 0 is no influence.

Constraints override parenting and object transforms. Let's parent the sphere to the cube and try to move the empty along the x-axis; nothing will happen (Image 9). In order to allow the sphere to influence the cube you need to disable the constraint (Image 10). By default a constraint replaces an object's transforms, but this can be changed (Image 11).

Like modifiers, constraints can be applied (Image 11); thia applies the transform to the object but removes the constraint for future changes. Constraints can also be duplicated. Constraints are applied in the same order as modifiers: top-to-bottom. In this example (Image 12), we see the cube get copy the transform values from the empty first, and then copy the transform from the sphere, which is the final result seen in the viewport. You can adjust the influence on multiple constraints to affect the results.

key_concepts: As any Blender object, it’s a container with trnasformation information.
It features specific datas : Armature data and bones data.
It has 3 modes, object, edit and pose.
You should always have your armature transform channels reset. before rigging anything.
Use bone constraint, not object constraint to build your rig.
[k]Tab[/k] = Enter/exit edit mode.
[k]Ctrl-Tab = Enter/exit pose mode.
Bone layers/collections, bone groups = organise your armature.

content: Armatures are objects in Blender. You can add one to you scene with [k]Shift-A > Armature[/k] and a bone will appear where the 3D cursor was. If your 3D cursor wasn't at the world origin when you added the armature, it will reflect that in the transform (Image 1). You will want to [k]Alt-R,Alt-S,Alt-G[/k] to clear all transforms on your armature. You want to create a rig with an armature that has no rotation, scale, or location offset; otherwise you could generate unexpected behavior when animating. It is a best practice to clear the transforms on both the armature and the mesh before rigging.

An armature is a blender object, and it has several components attached to it, such as Data properties, Bone properties, and Bone Constraints properties (Image 2). Armatures have three main modes. [k]Object Mode[/k] allows you to edit the armature's transforms. [k]Edit Mode[/k] is where you will set the orientation of different bones, add new bones, parent bones; basically create the structure of your armature. This is also where we set the Rest Pose for each bone. [k]Pose Mode[/k] is where we animate the armature and also add constraints.

In the [k]Data Propeties[/k] for an armature, you will see two different options: [k]Pose Position[/k] or [k]Rest Position[/k] (Image 4). This affects the position displayed in [k]Pose Mode[/k]. For example, let's create a simple armature and pose it (Image 5). While [k]Pose Position[/k] is toggled, we see the armature's latest pose; but if we toggle [k]Rest Position[/k] then the viewport goes back to the armature's Rest Pose (Image 6). You can clear a pose by using [k]Alt-R,Alt-S,Alt-G[/k] or [k]Pose > Clear Transform > All[/k].

Bone collections help you organize, hide, isolate, and manage rig bones; you can find your bone collections in the [k]Data Properties[/k] (Image 6). Bones are assigned to a collection with [k]M[/k], and removed with [k]Shift-M[/k]. Bones can be assigned to multiple collections. Collections are nestable, so collections can contain other collections.
You can change a bone's color under [k]Bone Properties > Viewport Display[/k] (Image 7).

key_concepts: By Default, an armature is made of a single bone. We can consider 3 families of bones:
Deformation bones = deform the mesh using Associated Vertex group influences.
Controller bones = Used by the animator to pose/animate an object.
Mechanism bones = USed to drive the deformation bones with the controllers and create complex mechanism.
The Bone’s head is its pivot point.
CTRL+R change bone roll. Twisting the bone around its local Y axis. In edit mode
Use Wire display mode for the armature object.
Use in Front to display the bones in front of any other object.
A bone can be considered as Vector, its size doesn’t matter, but there are exceptions.
B-Bones are unique to Blender and can’t be used by other softwares or game Engines.
They behave like a 2 vectors bezier curve.
Shift+W Toggle Deform.

content: There are different types of bones in Blender.
Controller bones are exposed to the animator allowing for character or rig posing and animation.

Deformation bones are driven by the controller bones and actually deform the character. They influence the vertices positions of the mesh. This influence can be shared by multiple bones for complex deformations. Deformation bone's influence can be adjusted using vertex groups to create complex deformations.
Vertex groups are a named group of vertices with an influence value. A signle vertex can belong to multiple vertex groups.
Mechanism bones are intermediate or helper bones in Blender that act as a bridge between your animator-facing Control bones and the actual Deformation bones that bend your mesh.

Bones have two ends: the tail (Image 1) and the head (Image 2). The head is the bone's pivot point. The section in the middle is the body (Image 3); this represents the length of the bone. The roll of the bone is controlled by its rotation; [k]Ctrl-R[/k] to rotate the bone around its y-axis (Image 4). Bone roll and orientation are very important in rigging, so make sure you stay aware.

You will want to see more information about the armature you are working on; go to the [k]Data Properties > Viewport Display[/k] and enable [k]Name[/k] and [k]Axes]/k] (Image 5). And go to [k]Object Properties > Viewport Display > Display As[/k] and set it to [k]Wire[/k] (Image 6). This will ensure your bones are transparent. The last setting is under [k]Data Properties > Viewport Display[/k] and enable [k]In Front[/k]; thie ensures your bone is always visible.
A bone at its heart is simply a vector; it has a position, an orientation, and a factor.
B-bones or bendy bones are a type of bone unique to Blender. They cannot be exported to a game engine. They are a special type of bone that can be manipulated as a 2 vector bezier curve.
